**February 20, 1952 — a Wednesday**

You arrived in the middle of an American winter that felt genuinely uncertain. Harry Truman was in the White House but had already decided not to run again. American soldiers were dying on frozen Korean hillsides, locked in a stalemate near the 38th parallel that armistice talks were failing to break. The Soviet Union had detonated its first atomic bomb two and a half years earlier. The shadow of mutual annihilation was not metaphor — it was strategic doctrine.

And yet the baby boom was roaring. Suburbs were spreading. Arguments in living rooms centered on whether to buy a television.

---

**The Oslo Winter Olympics — in progress on your birthday**

The VI Winter Olympics were underway in Oslo, Norway (February 14–25, 1952), meaning the Games were live on your birthday. A 19-year-old American alpine skier named Andrea Mead Lawrence was competing that week; she won two gold medals in slalom events, becoming the first American to claim two individual golds at a single Winter Games. The Olympics were still a largely radio-and-newsreel event — television coverage was a future dream. That would change completely within your first decade.

---

**Your 10th birthday: John Glenn orbits Earth**

On February 20, 1962 — your exact tenth birthday — Marine Corps pilot and astronaut John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth, completing three circuits aboard Friendship 7 before splashing down in the Atlantic. The timing is not symbolic; it is just true. On the morning you turned ten, a man was in orbit above you. The nation watched on television — the same medium that had barely existed when you were born. It is one of the more striking exact-date coincidences in the arc of any life begun in 1952.

---

**Television: the medium that grew up with you**

In early 1952, television sets were in roughly one in three American homes and still spreading rapidly. The medium was new enough that the political conventions of that summer — where Eisenhower secured the Republican nomination — were considered a bold experiment in live broadcast. By the time you were eight, TV had reshaped how America chose its presidents. By the time you were in high school, it had transmitted both the Moon landing and the Vietnam War into living rooms simultaneously. You are among the last generation for whom television's arrival is a childhood memory rather than an assumed fixture of birth.

---

**The transistor, unannounced**

Bell Labs demonstrated the transistor in late 1947. By early 1952, commercial production was beginning — quietly, without headlines, in a world still running on vacuum tubes. That small device seeded everything that followed: the integrated circuit, the personal computer, the internet, the smartphone. The trajectory from the transistor to the AI systems running in 2026 passed directly through your lifetime. You were born into a world of analog limits; you inhabit a world where those limits have largely dissolved and humanity is trying to understand what that actually means.

---

**±30 days: A queen ascends**

Fourteen days before your birth, on February 6, 1952, King George VI died in his sleep at Sandringham. His daughter — 25-year-old Princess Elizabeth, on safari in Kenya at the time — received the news and flew home as Queen Elizabeth II. Her coronation the following June became one of the first great shared global television events. Elizabeth II reigned for 70 years, dying in September 2022. Her reign began two weeks before you were born. She is, in a real sense, a figure who spans the entire conscious arc of your life from before its start to well within living memory.

---

**What you entered, what you witnessed**

You were born into a world of physical limits — limits on distance, on information, on who could speak to whom and how fast. Korea was the war no one had fully prepared for. The Bomb was real and new and terrifying. Television was still an argument. Computers occupied entire buildings and belonged to governments and corporations.

In 74 years you have watched: the Berlin Wall go up (1961) and come down (1989). Humans walk on the Moon. The Soviet Union dissolve. The internet go from military network to global nervous system. A device that fits in a shirt pocket now contains more computing capacity than existed in the entire world the day you were born.

The person who entered that February world of 1952 — anxious, Cold War-shadowed, but roaring with postwar possibility — has lived through one of the most compressed transformations in the history of human civilization. That is not a small thing to have witnessed firsthand.
